posts.content:
The most honest read on where this industry's headed isn't a report — it's what customers tell me on calls.

Lately, what I've been hearing a lot of is this: "What happens the other 350 days?"

Even just six months ago, a pentest was still an annual ritual — 15 days, tens of thousands of dollars, a PDF telling you what was wrong the week it happened to run. The other 350 days, you were flying blind.

That gap stopped being theoretical. HackerOne saw AI-generated vulnerability reports up 210% this year — prompt-injection reports alone, up 540%. Attackers aren't waiting for your next pentest window. They're reasoning about your application continuously, at machine speed.

You can't out-schedule that. So we stopped trying to.

This month, Snyk Evo Continuous Offensive Security went GA — AI pentesting and agent red teaming that test your applications every day of the year, not fifteen. Every finding is cleared by an independent validation judge and ships with a runnable proof of exploit, not a hunch.

One design partner said it best: "We can't schedule our way out of a continuous risk surface."

Neither can you.

Evo Continuous Offensive Security (COS) launched at Blackhat. The real work actually starts after the GA: At one of our enterprise customers today - an external firm spent 15 days pentesting this application. Evo COS spent 4 hours.

It found everything they found, plus what they missed.

That is a real enterprise run in a real production environment. 3 criticals surfaced. Security validated 2 as real and actionable. The first root caused to an unused agent service still deployed, deprecated the same day. The second was an auth-flow regression introduced by recent changes. The service owner confirmed it, used the remediation guidance, and shipped the fix immediately. Zero back-and-forth on validation, because the repro steps and the architecture view were clear enough that security and engineering read the same finding the same way. Two of the criticals matched their most recent external pentest. COS caught more.

The old math was never defensible. A 15-day engagement runs $15K to $50K and leaves roughly 350 days where every release ships untested at the flaw layer. Attackers stopped respecting that calendar. They have the same reasoning-capable models your developers have, and they probe business logic continuously at machine speed. Gartner expects the window to exploitation to halve by 2027. Every CISO I talk to is asking the same question now. How do we prepare for autonomous AI attacks.

At Black Hat we brought Evo Continuous Offensive Security to GA. Frontier models run the assessment under Snyk's offensive harness. A separate validation model acts as independent judge and confirms exploitability before anything reaches a human. Context from Snyk Code, Snyk Open Source, Snyk API & Web and AI-SPM aims the testing at architectural flaws instead of the bugs your scanners already caught. The generator cannot be the validator. That is the whole reason these findings survive contact with an engineer.

Note the unused agent service. Agents in production are attack surface now, and most programs cannot tell you what theirs can reach.

Now every Snyk customer can run this continuously instead of once a year.

The annual pentest as the unit of assurance is ending.

September 2, 11am ET. Ricardo Alves and John Carione run it live, and Gabriel Brolo of Yalo walks through what his team is actually solving.

posts.content:
When Snyk opened the Remediation Agent design partner program, I said the real value of AI in remediation was the CONTEXT it has, not the model itself.

Well, consider my statement validated.

I'm excited to share that the Remediation Agent is now in public preview, and it covers not just open source, but code as well (Container soon too!)

Against the same models running without Snyk's intelligence behind them, fix rates went up roughly 94% on SCA issues and roughly 14% on SAST.

Code is supposedly where a frontier model is already strongest on its own.

Didn't matter.

Fix quality still got measurably better once it knew what Snyk knows about the finding.

But...design partners didn't really push us on the fixes.

They pushed us on having confidence about the build. 

A fix that compiles and closes the CVE is worthless if the version bump takes down a service, and no amount of model reasoning tells you whether it will. 

To ACTUALLY address it, a company has to know how a package has behaved across every upgrade anyone's attempted. 

So our breakability scorer now runs before the agent even opens a PR, and if it's likely to break, Snyk will work with the agent to make the necessary adjustments in your codebase. 

Breaking changes turn to mergeable changes in two turns, not dozens, and not after hours of a developer's time.

This is the difference between a fix you ignore and a fix you merge.

This difference is how I saw Relay Network cut critical remediation time from more than a week to under 24 hours.

And there's plenty left to build. 

If you've got a backlog worth denting, I'd love for you to try it and tell me where it falls down. 

That feedback is what got us from the experiment to here, and is how we're going to get from where we are now to GA!

posts.content:
Snyk has signed the Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter with 270 other industry leaders (thanks to Microsoft for coordinating this important statement across the industry), and joined NVIDIA and the Open Secure AI Alliance. I want to share my thoughts on why this is important: 

Attackers do not have a terms of service.

They run open models on their own hardware. No rate limits, no refusals, nobody auditing what they asked for. Defenders file access requests for systems they are not allowed to inspect.

That is the argument people expect me to make, and it is the weakest of the three reasons I care about this.

Start with economics, because it decides everything else. Continuous defense means running models constantly rather than occasionally. Attack your applications continuously. Remediate continuously. Red team the agents continuously. At that duty cycle frontier per-token pricing does not survive contact with a real enterprise estate, which is why cost went from a procurement detail to a board conversation almost overnight. Open weights is part of what makes continuous affordable instead of aspirational.

Then safety, which is the part that surprises people. Our own risk intelligence red teams every version of the frontier and leading open models, and the result is not a leaderboard. It is a matrix. A model can follow instructions beautifully and leak PII badly. Alignment tuned for consumer safety will refuse work a security team legitimately needs done. There is no safest model. There is only the safest model for this job, and for some jobs the answer is an open one. A single vendor strategy is a bet that one model is best at everything, and the data does not support that bet.

Which is why defender disparity comes third. It is real, and Hugging Face is the sharpest example of it. But it is the one a vendor could choose to fix tomorrow. The other two are structural.

One more thing I said last week I would not ignore. The majority of software runs on open source. My read is that tens of thousands of undisclosed vulnerabilities already sit in private hands, found by groups pointing these capabilities at the commons, while maintainers drown in a mix of real reports and AI slop. That is how a commons caves under its own weight, and no amount of model access fixes it.

Open models are not a silver bullet. They are the difference between a defender who can act and one who can only ask.

The attacker does not sleep. And the defense cannot be built behind closed doors.

Why I think this is urgent: https://lnkd.in/e-gtx4tK

‼️Attackers stopped picking a layer.

Nearly every CISO conversation now starts with the same question:
“How do I prepare for the post-Mythos era—when autonomous AI attacks move from a research breakthrough to a mainstream attacker operating model?”

AI-driven development raises the rate at which risk is created. Autonomous attacks compress the time available to find and fix it. When your remediation rate is below your risk-creation rate, no individual tool changes the outcome. You are not getting safer. You are falling behind at a different speed.

So today at Black Hat, we did not ship another point product. We closed the loop. 🔄

💡Discover the real software and AI attack surface—models, agents, MCP servers, skills, tools and what each can reach—with upgraded AI-SPM.

➿Remediate the inherited backlog autonomously with the Evo Agentic AppSec remediation agent, now in public preview.

🛂Validate what is actually exploitable, continuously, with Evo Continuous Offensive Security, generally available today.

✋Prevent secrets and malicious packages from rebuilding the backlog as humans and agents write software, with Snyk Secrets now GA and malicious-code defense in private preview.

🔄 Four actions. One connected system.

A loop with a missing segment is not a loop. It is a gap an autonomous attacker will occupy.

At the center is COS, the adversarial proving layer.

We did not build it by pointing a model at an application and calling it a pentester.

Nuno Loureiro and the team spent their careers as software penetration testers, then put decades of that judgment into a multi-agent harness plus leveraging our years of global context and unique local context from the software pipelines that we are already deployed in at the largest enterprises.

One agent finds. Another must independently reproduce it before you ever see it. Others chain low-impact findings into the outcome a real attacker would pursue.

Nothing has general internet access. Scope is enforced by the environment, not by a prompt.

On a large enterprise design partner customer’s multi-tenant sales enablement platform—black box, staging, almost no documentation—it worked out what the application was for, then found a path that let a standard user rewrite tenant-wide security configuration.

Password policy. Upload denylist. Even the OAuth integration.

That is not a scanner finding.

Gabriel Brolo at Yalo said it better than our copy did:

You cannot schedule your way out of a continuous risk surface.

The open standard last week.
The evidence yesterday.
The system today.

That order was deliberate.

posts.content:
Capability is not a security score. An approved model list is not AI governance.

Snyk published Volume II of the State of Agentic AI Adoption today. Not survey data. Observed enterprise telemetry across 3,044 accounts and 1.39 million repositories (leveraging our built in Snyk platform Evo AIBOM capabilities). Model inventories capture about a third of the real AI footprint, so most governance programs are working from a third of the picture.

And the visible third is fragmenting. OpenAI fell from 43.6% to 34.0% of observed model occurrences in six months. The open ecosystem more than doubled. Open weights now sit roughly four months behind the closed frontier, close enough that cost, latency, resilience and sovereignty change the answer.

Finding the model is step one. The decision is which model version is allowed for which use case, at what risk threshold, and how that rule holds.

An HR assistant needs the model least likely to leak employee PII under attack. A customer-facing agent needs one that holds its role when someone works to override it. Is that the newest frontier release, or GLM, or Kimi? Capability benchmarks tell you what a model can accomplish. They do not tell you what an attacker can make it do.

That is what the Risk Intelligence Agent in Evo AI-SPM answers. It adversarially tests and scores model versions on attack success rate rather than vendor claims, across five security categories, broken down to attacker goals like PII extraction, decision override and tool misuse. It tests realistic deployment contexts, because the same model is a different risk as a coding agent, an internal data agent or a customer-facing chatbot. And it scores per version, because the model you validated in March is not the model you are running today.

Then the Policy Agent turns that into a rule in plain English. No model above this PII extraction threshold in any application touching employee records. It enforces inside the SDLC and ADLC workflows Snyk is already embedded in. No separate gate. No new policy syntax.

Discover the real AI surface. Measure the risk that matters. Enforce the decision.

Obviously, model choice narrows risk, it does not remove it. A weaker model inside a bounded least privilege runtime beats a stronger one holding broad credentials.

Nvidia and 36 other companies launched the Open Secure AI Alliance last week. It follows the $12.5M the Linux Foundation raised earlier this year from Anthropic, AWS, GitHub, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI, pointed specifically at helping maintainers triage and remediate what's coming at them.

The remediate half is the part worth watching, in my (not so) humble opinion.

Finding vulnerabilities in open source is nearly free now. 

Every scanner will do it, and in fact, plenty will be more than happy to open an issue on your repo without being asked. 

Now a volunteer with a day job has 400 findings they didn't ask for and can't get through.

But the exposure is growing from both directions. 

AI writes more code, which pulls in more dependencies, which widens the surface. 

And Mythos showed that the lows everyone was trained to triage away chain into criticals, so "prioritize better" has stopped being a real answer.

The entire industry is built on open source software and almost nobody pays for it.

Thankfully, Snyk gives open source maintainers full enterprise licenses for free through the Secure Developer Program. Over 585,000 projects have taken us up on it. 

At RAISE this month Manoj Nair committed to also putting our latest release, the AI-driven remediation agent, in their hands for free as well. 

Excited that my team's a part of this next wave in securing open source, because getting what we've built to maintainers is, again in my not so humble opinion, the most useful thing we can do with it.

posts.content:
Over 100 companies signed an open letter today saying we have a limited window on cyber defense. Snyk signed it. The most important word in that letter is "verified." Nothing in it says who does the verifying.

That question is the whole game now.

AI made finding vulnerabilities close to free. It made trusting your software expensive. If the model that writes the fix also certifies the fix, we have not reduced risk. We have industrialized unverified change at machine speed. The generator cannot be the validator. That is not a vendor position, it is separation of duties applied to machines, and it applies to the agents we build too.

Every CISO I talk to is asking a version of the same question: how do I know the fix is real?

That is what we are building into the Snyk platform. 
✅ Deterministic validation, independent of whatever wrote the code. 
✅ Frontier reasoning grounded in Snyk Security Intelligence, so the model reasons over confirmed findings instead of plausible ones. 
✅ The Remediation Agent applies the fix, rescans, runs your existing tests, then hands your engineer the PR. A human still signs off. The output is a fix that survived a check, not a suggestion that joins the backlog.

Labelbox cleared a two-year backlog in weeks running this workflow. Now every Snyk customer can run the same loop.

And the internet's first line of defense is still unpaid open source maintainers. They should not be doing this with consumer-grade tools. Through our Secure Developer Program, qualifying maintainers get a Snyk account with full enterprise entitlements and no usage limits. The same product our largest customers run.

Apply: https://lnkd.in/eNkm2rtJ

Signing a letter is the easy part. Put capable defense in more hands, then measure progress by issues fixed, not issues found.
